title: Cesar Figueroa
text: I am a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia, and before that I spent six years as an accountant in Vancouver. I grew up in Barranquilla, Colombia, studied public accounting at Universidad del Norte, and moved to Canada to keep building on that work. Years of closing books and chasing down numbers that did not add up taught me that the interesting part was never the reconciliation itself, but the question underneath it. I am here to learn how to answer those questions properly, with data.

title: Penguin flipper length and body mass

Data source

title: Penguin flipper length and body mass
text:
Check data quality
I check for missing values in flipper length and body mass before examining their relationship.

measurements <- penguins[c("flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g")]

nrow(measurements)

[1] 344

colSums(is.na(measurements))

flipper_length_mm       body_mass_g 
                2                 2

title: Penguin flipper length and body mass
text:
Prepare the data
I retain observations with both flipper length and body mass available. Missing values in other variables do not affect this selection.

measurements_clean <- measurements[complete.cases(measurements), ]

nrow(measurements_clean)

[1] 342

nrow(measurements) - nrow(measurements_clean)

[1] 2

title: Penguin flipper length and body mass
text:
Visualize the relationship
Each point represents one penguin with both measurements available.

plot(
  measurements_clean$flipper_length_mm,
  measurements_clean$body_mass_g,
  xlab = "Flipper length (mm)",
  ylab = "Body mass (g)",
  pch = 19,
  col = "steelblue"
)







Figure 1: Flipper length and body mass for 342 penguins with complete measurements.

title: Penguin flipper length and body mass
text:
Measure the association
I calculate Pearson’s correlation to summarize the linear association between flipper length and body mass.

correlation <- cor(
  measurements_clean$flipper_length_mm,
  measurements_clean$body_mass_g
)

round(correlation, 3)

[1] 0.871

title: Penguin flipper length and body mass
text:
Findings :O
Among the 342 penguins with both measurements available, flipper length and body mass have a Pearson correlation of 0.871. This indicates a strong positive linear association, consistent with the upward pattern in Figure 1.
This analysis combines three species. Differences between species may contribute to the overall association, so the result does not necessarily describe the relationship within each species. Correlation does not establish that longer flippers cause greater body mass. Two observations with missing measurements were excluded.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Classes started on August 31st, and the first thing I noticed was the pace. Four courses running at once, lectures in the morning and labs every afternoon at two, and a new topic arriving before the previous one has finished settling. Coming from six years of accounting, where the calendar is built around a monthly close I could see coming from a week away, this is a different rhythm entirely.



Campus during my first weeks in the MDS program.


The surprise has not been the statistics or the programming. It has been how much of the work is infrastructure: SSH keys, version control, rendering pipelines, getting four different tools to agree on where a file lives. I spent part of a weekend on an SSH connection that timed out over and over, and the fix turned out to have nothing to do with my key. That was frustrating at the time and useful in retrospect, because nobody hands you a working environment in real work either.
Right now I feel busy and slightly behind, which I gather is the normal state here. What I am looking forward to is the point where the tools stop being the obstacle and become the thing I reach for without thinking about it.

title: Comparing penguin body mass across species
text:
Check data quality
Before comparing species, I check the dataset size and count missing values in the variables needed for this analysis.

print(f"Number of rows: {penguins.shape[0]}")
penguins[["species", "body_mass_g"]].isna().sum()

Number of rows: 344


species        0
body_mass_g    2
dtype: int64

title: Comparing penguin body mass across species
text:
Prepare the data
Two observations have missing body mass (Na). I exclude these two rows from the comparison and keep observations with missing values in unrelated columns.

penguins_clean = penguins.dropna(subset=["body_mass_g"]).copy()

print(f"Original rows: {len(penguins)}")
print(f"Rows retained: {len(penguins_clean)}")
print(f"Rows removed: {len(penguins) - len(penguins_clean)}")

Original rows: 344
Rows retained: 342
Rows removed: 2

title: Comparing penguin body mass across species
text:
Compare body mass across species
I calculate the number of observations, mean, and median body mass for each species. Body mass is measured in grams.

mass_summary = (
    penguins_clean.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .agg(["count", "mean", "median"])
    .round(1)
)

mass_summary

title: Comparing penguin body mass across species
text:
Findings :O
Gentoo penguins have the highest mean body mass in this sample: approximately 5,076 g, compared with 3,701 g for Adelie and 3,733 g for Chinstrap. The median follows the same pattern: 5,000 g for Gentoo and 3,700 g for both other species.
These are descriptive comparisons of the observed penguins. They do not establish that species alone explains the differences; this analysis does not account for factors such as sex, island, or year. Two observations with missing body mass were excluded.

title: Comparing penguin body mass across species
text:
Visualize body mass
The boxplot compares the median, spread, and potential outliers of body mass across species.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

species = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]
mass_by_species = [
    penguins_clean.loc[
        penguins_clean["species"] == name, "body_mass_g"
    ]
    for name in species
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.boxplot(mass_by_species, tick_labels=species)
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Distribution of body mass by species, excluding two observations with missing body mass.

title: About
text:
Why data science
Accounting gave me a lot of time with messy data and very little time with the questions I actually wanted to ask of it. I kept building spreadsheets that were really analyses in disguise, and eventually started learning SQL and Python on my own to do the job properly. The MDS program is the deliberate version of that detour: I want to move from reporting what happened to explaining why, and from static reports to tools other people can use.
